analysis.one_liner: Gives landowners stronger notice, compensation, and appeal rights when natural gas pipelines use eminent domain.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by two Senate Democrats to tighten pipeline permitting and eminent domain rules, was referred to committee in August 2020 and never received a vote before the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change how federal natural gas pipeline permits work under the Natural Gas Act. Companies seeking a pipeline permit would have to give landowners clearer, earlier notice — with step-by-step instructions on how to intervene and preserve their right to go to court — at least 60 days before the deadline. Companies could not start construction or seize land through eminent domain until every appeal had been resolved and every federal and state permit was in hand. Courts weighing compensation would have to count the loss of a property's conservation value, appraisals would have to meet professional standards with the owner allowed to accompany the appraiser, and offers could not fall below appraised fair market value. It would also force regulators to study nearby pipeline projects together, hold public meetings in every affected county, and account for visual damage to national scenic trails.
analysis.who_benefits: Landowners in the path of interstate natural gas pipelines, who today often receive terse legal notice, lowball offers, and lose access to court if they miss a narrow intervention window. Communities along pipeline routes gain guaranteed public meetings in their own counties and cumulative environmental review when multiple projects cluster within 100 miles. Holders of conservation easements — including landowners who gave up development rights for tax benefits or conservation purposes — gain compensation for the value that a pipeline taking destroys. Users of national scenic trails gain visual-impact simulations and cumulative analysis of clustered projects.

how_it_helps.text: Notices to landowners must be approved by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, served at least 60 days before the intervention deadline, and must plainly state in bold print that intervening in the proceeding is the only way to preserve the right to judicial review [S3].

A certificate holder cannot begin an eminent domain action until all timely applications for rehearing have received a ruling or been deemed denied, and a court cannot grant the taking until the company holds every federal and state permit needed to build and complete the entire project [S3].
In setting just compensation for land under a conservation easement, courts must consider the 'lost conservation value' — the interrupted conservation use and any resulting drop in land value [S3].

Appraisals must follow generally accepted standards before any offer is made, the owner may accompany the appraiser, offers must be in writing at no less than appraised fair market value including damages to adjacent property, and a court cannot even hear an eminent domain petition unless appraisal and offer requirements were met [S3].
Applications for rehearing are deemed denied after 45 days, which opens the door to prompt judicial review instead of letting the agency sit on appeals [S3].

Two pipeline applications filed within a year, in the same state and within 100 miles, must be treated as one project for environmental review; public meetings must be held in each county a project crosses; and environmental impact statements must include leaf-on and leaf-off visual simulations for national scenic trails [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Natural gas pipeline developers, who would face longer timelines, higher land-acquisition costs, more litigation exposure, and a harder path to assembling rights-of-way. In practice some of those costs could flow through to gas customers in rates, and projects that no longer pencil out under the stricter rules simply would not be built — which the bill's sponsors would count as a feature and the industry a cost.

drawbacks.text: Requiring every permit and every rehearing to be resolved before any construction or eminent domain action could extend project timelines substantially, and critics of permitting delays argue this raises costs that flow to gas ratepayers and can kill infrastructure that serves energy reliability [S3].

Treating projects within 100 miles as one for environmental review and barring national forest plan amendments that degrade scenic trail resources could foreclose pipeline routes through broad swaths of Appalachian terrain, pushing costs onto landowners elsewhere along rerouted paths [S3].

The bill never advanced past committee, so it received no hearing or amendment process where these tradeoffs could be weighed, and its single-chamber, two-sponsor start gave it no base of support to build from [S1] [S5].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protections are well-targeted at a real, documented imbalance: landowners facing a federally backed pipeline company with eminent domain power often lose legal rights through procedural fine print. The main cost is slower, costlier pipeline permitting, which falls partly on gas customers and partly on the industry. The bill is modest in scale — it does not ban pipelines, it disciplines how they are built — but it also arrived with almost no political support, which is the honest reason it went nowhere.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in August 2020, read twice, and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Tim Kaine, joined by Sen. Mark Warner, introduced the bill on August 6, 2020, framing it as a way to bolster fairness and transparency in interstate natural gas pipeline permitting [S1] [S3].
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation [S5].
No further action appears in the record — the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and it died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Natural gas pipeline developers are better off, since they keep the existing permitting process, notice practices, and eminent domain powers the bill would have restricted. Landowners along pipeline routes, who the bill was written for, are left with the status quo.

sides.party_line_note: Only two Democratic senators sponsored the bill, no senator is on record opposing it, and it never came to a vote, so the partisan shape of support and opposition cannot be measured.

industries.note: The bill would have lengthened permitting timelines, barred eminent domain and construction until all permits and appeals are resolved, and raised land-acquisition costs through mandatory appraisals and conservation-value compensation. Its death leaves the industry's existing advantages over landowners intact.

Utilities rely on the interstate pipelines this bill would have made slower and costlier to build, so some of the compliance cost could surface in gas rates. The bill did not restrict gas use itself, only how pipelines are sited and built.
